title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 10: Start Electoral Reforms Now
keywords: Comelec Chair Jose A. R. Melo
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's January 2, 2011 Inquirer column urging President Aquino to 'start electoral reforms now,' since (unlike the Court, where he can name only four of 15 justices) he can reshape the Commission on Elections through a 'sweeping revamp' of its membership

The opening to revamp the Comelec -- with Chairman Melo's resignation and two commissioners' retirements, P-Noy could 'appoint immediately three of the seven' members (including the chair), and two more in 2013, enough to 'dominate the poll body' -- ahead of the May 2013 elections

The new Comelec's three challenges -- first, whether to keep automation at all (weighing speed against 'humongous expense,' and Monsod's doubts about the 'non-transparent' P16.5-billion PCOS that left 'traditional' cheating untouched); second, if automation continues, what system (with Monsod, the watchdog Lente, and the Comelec Advisory Council all panning the PCOS); and third, time

His warning that, with the 2013 polls 'just two and a half years' away and the PCOS possibly to be jettisoned, time is 'barely enough' -- recalling the 2010 timetable that was 'almost always tardy' (ballot, delivery and calibration delays), and noting Roque v. Comelec had settled the automation contract's legality but not its 'technical, administrative, and logistical' woes
sub_topics: Why the Comelec, not the Court: in six years Aquino can name only four of the 15 justices, 'not enough to sway a new judicial philosophy,' but he 'can initiate electoral reforms via a sweeping revamp' of the Comelec

The appointment opening: with Chairman Jose A. R. Melo resigning at month's end and Commissioners Nicodemo Ferrer and Gregorio Larrazabal retiring in February, P-Noy could 'appoint immediately three of the seven Comelec members, including the pivotal chairman,' and two more in February 2013, ultimately naming five who 'would clearly dominate the poll body'

The 2010 verdict: despite 'many problems,' the PCOS-aided polls were held 'in relative peace and order' and the results, 'especially of the presidential contest, were accepted' -- though 'more electoral protests were filed... in the last automated derby than in the previous manual elections'

Challenge one -- whether to automate: the Comelec must weigh automation's 'advantage of speed' against its 'humongous expense and difficulties,' with its inputs 'most persuasive' to Congress; Monsod questioned the 'non-transparent and secretive' way the PCOS counted ballots 'beyond the scrutiny of the public,' noted the 'very expensive (P16.5 billion)' system 'did not address the traditional problems' (cheating, command votes, disenfranchisement, low registration), and argued that solving those might mean 'the country may not need an expensive automation system'

Challenge two -- which system: if the Court 'declares automation constitutional,' what system to adopt -- Monsod 'unequivocally trashed' the PCOS as 'mass-produced in one step,' inadequately 'pilot-tested,' from a supplier with no 'extensive experience'; the watchdog Lente found that 'peaceful and expedient elections did not translate to honest and credible elections,' with 'vote-buying' and intimidation 'most prevalent'; and the Comelec Advisory Council said the body 'is better off not exercising the option to purchase the PCOS machines'
Challenge three -- time: the May 2013 election is 'just two and a half years' away, and if the PCOS 'should be jettisoned,' the Comelec is 'really pressed for time' to start anew

The 2010 cautionary timeline: Melo took over March 25, 2008, about two years before the 2010 polls -- about the same runway a February-2011 appointee would have for 2013 -- yet the Comelec, though it had 'a strict, step-by-step timetable,' was 'almost always tardy,' with 'horrifying delays' in ballot printing, delivery and PCOS calibration

The legal vs. logistical: Roque v. Comelec had 'upheld the automation contract' with Smartmatic, putting 'to rest the legal questions, but not the technical, administrative, and logistical issues' -- so, with 'only two years and a few months' left, 'barely enough to prepare,' Aquino, Congress, the Comelec and the watchdogs 'should now carefully plan for the 2013 elections'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's January 2, 2011 Inquirer column, urges President Aquino to 'start electoral reforms now.' Unlike the Court -- where in six years he can name only four of 15 justices, 'not enough to sway a new judicial philosophy' -- Aquino can reshape the Commission on Elections through a 'sweeping revamp': with Chairman Melo resigning and Commissioners Ferrer and Larrazabal retiring, he could 'appoint immediately three of the seven' members (including the chair) and two more in 2013, enough to 'dominate the poll body.' The 2010 polls, CJP allows, were held 'in relative peace,' and the results -- 'especially of the presidential contest' -- were 'accepted,' though more protests were filed than under manual elections. He sets the new Comelec three challenges. First, whether to automate at all: weighing speed against 'humongous expense,' he cites former Chair Christian Monsod's doubts about the 'non-transparent and secretive' P16.5-billion PCOS that 'did not address the traditional problems' of cheating, command votes and disenfranchisement -- so 'the country may not need an expensive automation system.' Second, if automation continues, which system: Monsod 'trashed' the PCOS as 'mass-produced in one step' and under-tested; the watchdog Lente found that 'peaceful and expedient elections did not translate to honest and credible elections,' with vote-buying 'most prevalent'; and the Comelec Advisory Council urged against buying the PCOS machines. Third, time: with May 2013 'just two and a half years' away and the PCOS perhaps to be jettisoned, the body is 'really pressed.' Recalling that Melo had about a two-year runway for 2010 yet the Comelec was 'almost always tardy' (with 'horrifying delays' in printing, delivery and calibration), and that Roque v. Comelec had settled the contract's legality 'but not the technical, administrative, and logistical issues,' he concludes that 'only two years and a few months remain' -- 'barely enough' -- so Aquino, Congress, the Comelec and the watchdogs 'should now carefully plan for the 2013 elections.'
